AI Beats Human Experts at Research Experiments: TasteVal Benchmark Confirms | Jackie Manning, Techtimes

A new AI benchmark has produced the first direct, quantified evidence that frontier AI systems have surpassed human experts at the core of scientific research work — designing experiments and interpreting their results — reaching expert-level performance at less than half the compute cost and at roughly one-thirtieth the per-attempt expense of a human researcher. The finding, from P-Zero Research's TasteVal benchmark published October 5 measures what the field calls "research taste" — the combination of skills that distinguishes productive scientific research from capable task execution.

The benchmark's best result came from Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, which achieved a compute multiplier of 2.30 against a human expert baseline of 24 researchers recruited from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Nvidia, and Microsoft Research. The 95 percent confidence interval for that figure spans from 1.15 to 4.37 — wide enough to span the difference between marginal superiority and decisive advantage, but with the entire range above the parity threshold of 1.0. Across multiple frontier model generations, the capability TasteVal measures has roughly doubled every three months since December 2025, compared to a doubling time of approximately 14 months before that period — a phase transition the benchmark's authors treat as among their most significant findings.

The benchmark deliberately and explicitly excludes one dimension of research judgment: choosing which problem to work on in the first place. That gap, which TasteVal's own authors identify as a remaining and unmeasured frontier, is the central limit on what the results can say about how close AI systems are to automating scientific research entirely.

What Recursive Self-Improvement Means

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is the threshold at which an AI system can train a more powerful successor entirely without human involvement — not automation of individual research tasks, but a closed loop in which a smarter model helps build a still-smarter model, potentially compressing decades of incremental progress. The concept has a lineage reaching back to I.J. Good's 1965 paper on ultraintelligent machines and Alan Turing's earlier "child machine" proposal; Eliezer Yudkowsky popularized the term "seed AI" to describe the self-replicating recursive improvement form of the phenomenon.

The question of when RSI becomes achievable has gained urgency as measurable proxies have appeared. Anthropic publicly reported that over 80 percent of merged code at the company was generated by AI models by May 2026. OpenAI announced in September 2026 that its research agents were logging approximately 3.1 agent-workdays of effort for each 8-hour human workday, though over half of successful 4-to-8-hour tasks still required human intervention. A September 28 paper co-authored by researchers including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, Jakub Pachocki, and Jack Clark found that AI's share of lightly supervised R&D work had risen from 1 percent to 26 percent between March and August 2026.

TasteVal enters this landscape as the first benchmark specifically designed to measure the judgment component of research work — not task completion speed or code generation, but the skill of designing experiments and interpreting what they show.

How TasteVal Measures Research Judgment

The architecture behind TasteVal is built around a deliberate conceptual separation. Scientific research judgment, the benchmark's authors argue, has three interlocking components: identifying which problems are worth pursuing; designing experiments to answer those problems; and correctly interpreting what the experimental results mean. TasteVal measures the second and third of these. The first — problem selection — is explicitly outside the benchmark's scope in this iteration.

To isolate judgment from coding ability, TasteVal uses a Researcher/Coder split architecture. The AI model under evaluation acts as the Researcher: it proposes experiments and draws conclusions from results. A fixed external Coder agent handles all implementation on a single Nvidia H100 GPU. Each run is capped at 40 GPU-hours of compute or 120 wall-clock hours, whichever comes first. This structure means a model cannot compensate for poor experimental judgment by writing faster or more efficient code — the coding work is held constant across all models.

The benchmark spans eight tasks drawn from frontier AI development work, covering training data selection, pretraining, fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and defense against adversarial prompts. The human baseline was constructed from 24 experts who had recently held research positions at OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Nvidia, and Microsoft Research, with at least two experts assigned to each task. TasteVal uses the best human result per task as the bar to beat — not the average — which sets a high baseline while also meaning the benchmark measures against expert floor performance rather than median researcher output.

Performance is expressed as a compute multiplier: the ratio of compute a human expert used to complete a task, divided by the compute the model required to reach the same score. A multiplier above 1.0 means the model reached expert-level performance using less computation than the human. Claude Opus 5.5's multiplier of 2.30 means it achieved expert-level results while spending roughly 43 percent of the compute a human expert used, at approximately one-thirtieth the per-attempt cost.

The Phase Transition Since December 2025

Among TasteVal's most significant findings is not the absolute level of performance but the shape of the improvement curve. Before approximately December 2025, the compute multiplier for research taste in frontier models doubled roughly every 14 months — consistent with gradual capability improvement. Since that period, the doubling time has compressed to approximately 3.0 months, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.7 to 5.0 months.

The TasteVal paper does not name a cause for this phase transition. One possible explanation, not stated in the paper but consistent with the timing and the broader institutional data, is that this inflection corresponds to the period in which AI systems began using other AI systems as research instruments in significant volume. Anthropic's own report on AI-generated code share — which rose from low single digits in early 2025 to over 80 percent of merged code by May 2026 — and the Cambridge paper's finding that AI's R&D automation share rose from 1 to 26 percent in the five months from March to August 2026 together suggest a feedback dynamic in which AI assists in AI research, accelerating the development of AI research capability itself. If that mechanism is driving the TasteVal doubling rate, it would not necessarily slow as human researcher productivity saturates — which is what makes the phase transition the most consequential element of the benchmark's findings.

The TasteVal paper is explicit that these results may overstate the trend. Because TasteVal tasks are scored quickly and cheaply, they are precisely the kind of task that AI labs find easiest to optimize for — raising the possibility that the steep improvement curve reflects benchmark-specific optimization as much as genuine underlying capability growth.

Where the Benchmark Deliberately Stops

The capability TasteVal measures is not the whole of what research taste means. Choosing which scientific problem to pursue — from a vast, open-ended space of possible research directions — is generally considered the deepest expression of scientific judgment, and it is explicitly outside TasteVal's scope.

This gap is substantiated by separate research. A 2026 study on AI post-training behavior found that AI agents in research settings locked into their initial strategy early in a task, with only 2.1 percent of training runs revising their committed approach; experience improved execution but not strategy revision. The paper identified the missing capability as the decision to reopen a committed strategy and consider an alternative — precisely the kind of problem-level judgment that TasteVal's task structure removes from the model's plate by pre-specifying the research goal.

The Anthropic alignment team's own separate TASTE benchmark, published August 28, provides a complementary data point. Anthropic's TASTE (not to be confused with TasteVal) measures AI models' ability to select the more promising of two AI safety research proposals — directly testing problem selection, the dimension TasteVal excludes. On that benchmark, the best-performing AI model tested (Claude Fable 5) scored approximately 60 percent against an estimated 77 percent for human researchers, a gap that remains substantial. Taken together, TasteVal and Anthropic's TASTE mark the boundary: AI has likely crossed or approached expert level at experiment design and result interpretation; it has not yet done so at research agenda selection.

There is also a structural limitation in TasteVal's human baseline. Using the best human result per task, rather than representative results, means the benchmark measures against the floor of expert performance — not the ceiling of what the best researchers in the world would produce with unlimited time and context.

How Clark Applied These Findings to His Forecast

Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic and author of the widely-read Import AI newsletter, updated his forecast for RSI in the newsletter's 476th edition, published October 12. Clark wrote that he now believes RSI — which he defines as a closed-loop system capable of training a more powerful successor with "no-human-involved" training — is now more likely in 2027 than in 2028, a compression of the timeline he had set as recently as May.

In May, in Import AI #455, Clark had put the probability at roughly 60 percent by end of 2028 and 30 percent by end of 2027. His October update revised the directional judgment without updating the probability figures — he stated only that his "more likely" year had shifted. The distinction matters: Clark is forecasting possibility, not inevitability. Whether any lab pursues RSI if and when it becomes technically possible depends on compute availability, safety frameworks, competitive dynamics, and regulatory context.

Clark cited two categories of evidence for the update: TasteVal's findings on AI research capability, and a wave of reports of AI systems producing what he described as "creative-seeming math breakthroughs."

A disclosure is worth stating clearly. Clark co-founded Anthropic, the organization whose model leads the TasteVal leaderboard. The benchmark comes from P-Zero Research, an independent group, but the most prominent person drawing forward-looking conclusions from it is affiliated with the top-performing lab. Clark's newsletter is his personal publication and does not represent Anthropic's official position. Clark also co-authored the September 28 Cambridge intelligence explosion paper in a personal capacity — not as an Anthropic representative — alongside Hinton, Bengio, and others who have called for governments to establish mandatory reporting on AI R&D automation levels, independent auditors inside AI companies, and emergency capability-pause mechanisms.

Clark's NAIAC membership, his 2023 briefing of the UN Security Council on AI threats, and his decade of work on AI policy mean his updated forecast carries weight in governance discussions — and that weight should be assessed against both the benchmark data he cites and the institutional position from which he makes it.

What the TasteVal Paper's Own Projections Show

The TasteVal paper goes further than Clark's newsletter in spelling out potential implications, using what the authors call the "AI Futures Model" developed by the AI Futures Project. The projections are labeled throughout as "naive extrapolation rather than a forecast" — the authors are explicit that these numbers should not be treated as predictions.

If the observed TasteVal improvement rate continues uninterrupted, the model calculates that the probability of what the paper calls a "taste-only singularity" — a scenario in which research taste improvements alone trigger recursive acceleration — would rise from 51 percent to 88 percent. The median projected arrival of artificial superintelligence (ASI) in this model shifts from 2030.5 to 2028.9; the probability of ASI before 2030 shifts from 46 percent to 69 percent.

The caveats the authors attach to these projections are substantive: the doubling rate is uncertain (confidence interval: 1.7 to 5.0 months), the tasks may be gameable, and the extrapolation applies only if the observed trend holds and only to the taste component of the broader RSI picture. Problem selection, multi-week planning, and real-world experimental execution are not reflected in these numbers.

The Counterarguments

The benchmarks' findings are contested, and the primary challenges point to exactly the limits already identified in the benchmark's design.

AI safety researcher Herbie Bradley's argument, which became a touchstone in the RSI debate following Clark's May essay, holds that AI systems had not demonstrated "research taste, genuine creativity, and coherent long-term research planning" at a level relevant to RSI. TasteVal directly challenges the experiment-design component of that claim. It says nothing about the third element Bradley named: coherent long-term research planning and problem selection.

The benchmark's Researcher/Coder split architecture, while solving the problem of isolating judgment from coding ability, also creates a task structure that differs from how actual research is conducted. Real research involves choosing what to build and revising that choice in light of unexpected results — precisely the capability the post-training study found AI agents were missing. A model optimized to perform well within a pre-specified research goal may not generalize to open-ended research agenda setting.

Ajeya Cotra at METR distinguishes three thresholds in AI research capability: adequacy (AI can do some research tasks without humans), parity (AI-only matches human-AI collaboration), and supremacy (AI-only outperforms human-AI collaboration). TasteVal's results speak to experiment-level adequacy and possibly parity on specific task types, not to overall research parity. Helen Toner at CSET has argued that using AI tools in AI research does not qualify as RSI under the classic definition, which requires that no humans are involved — a threshold not approached by any current system.

Broader Institutional Context

Clark's revised timeline arrives in a period of rapid institutional repositioning. Anthropic publicly acknowledged in June 2026 that RSI has not yet been achieved but warned that it "could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for." OpenAI, releasing its research automation data in September, was explicit that reaching measurable automation in research tasks does not mean RSI is a goal worth pursuing without human oversight in place.

The Cambridge intelligence explosion paper — the one co-authored by Clark, Hinton, Bengio, Pachocki, Eric Horvitz, and Dawn Song, among more than 20 researchers in total — made concrete policy asks tied directly to the data it presents. The paper's call for government-mandated reporting on AI R&D automation, independent auditors embedded in AI labs, and emergency pause mechanisms was grounded in the empirical finding that AI's share of lightly supervised R&D work had risen from 1 percent to 26 percent in five months. TasteVal's results, published three weeks after that paper, add a specific capability measurement to the empirical backdrop the Cambridge authors were working from.

What has changed is the evidentiary basis of the debate. The argument about RSI timelines has historically been driven by extrapolation from general-purpose benchmarks — reasoning scores, coding ability, task-completion duration. TasteVal represents an attempt to build a purpose-built instrument for the specific capability that matters most: whether AI systems can function as productive research scientists, not just productive coders or document processors. Its findings are not conclusive. Its methodology is contested. Its extrapolations are explicitly labeled speculative. But as a signal that the RSI debate has moved from abstract forecasting to measurement, it is a shift worth tracking carefully.

Daily Brief, 27 Oct: Does the market like the Anthropic S1?

Get the brief by email: https://t.co/vLaSSMqC6k
Join Rekt Mkts Pro: https://t.co/tpKPk67feu

Anthropic filed its S1 yesterday as it gears for plans to IPO in mid-November. I suppose the fact that they still intend to go ahead with it is bullish, and signals demand is there...altho it's still early days (WeWork often plays thru my head...one that kinda fucked me...a story for another time). It would seem that equities were bulled up by the move, with many AI stocks squeezing hard yesterday, while crypto saw a day of underperformance vs stocks.

MACRO
The Fed begins its two-day meeting today, with the decision due tomorrow. Today's consumer confidence and new home sales reports give us another check on demand before that decision. Conference Board confidence is expected at 80.5 versus 81.9 previously; although I don't expect a huge amount of volatility from the number.

The US 10Y is currently at 5% mostly unch'd, while the 30Y is around 5.30%, also unch'd. December WTI futures are around $101, down 0.8%, while gold futures are around $4,030, down 0.2%.

Generally I'm not expecting too many red herrings this week and I think midterms + ANT are the things that are most important here.

EQUITIES
S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 futures are higher, with tech leading. Korean memory has joined in much more convincingly than yday: SK Hynix finished up 5.2% and Samsung 4.2%, after both closed lower on Monday. Micron finished Monday up 3% and Nvidia 2.4%, so the US chip recovery did make it beyond the premarket gains and are set to open tepidly higher today. A successful ANT IPO would obviously be very bullish for AI stocks across the board after a rough few sessions; there's still a lot of moving parts and multiple scenarios of what could happen, but so far it's been a decent start given the reaction to the S1.

After yday's discussion about access to funding, that's a concrete deal for the market to respond to. It shows substantial capital is still available for this particular customer and structure, not that every neocloud can borrow on the same terms. Microsoft and Alphabet report tomorrow, followed by Amazon on Thursday. The useful question is how much of the spending is turning into cloud revenue and cash generation...a financed chip purchase is good news for the supplier, but the customer still needs to earn enough from the capacity.

CRYPTO
BTC is down around 0.4% over 24H, ETH 0.3% and SOL 1.4%, while HYPE is up 1.2%. HYPE is still leading this group as it did in yday's brief, but SOL has gone from joining the bounce to lagging the other majors. BTC and ETH haven't fallen much; they just aren't doing much with the stronger backdrop in stocks either.

VVV is up around 3% over 24H and ZEC 1.4%, so both are holding up better than BTC, with VVV now ahead of ZEC on the daily move. Their BTC ratios are up roughly 3.5% and 1.8% respectively over the same period and the strength has certainly been notable as BTC continues to barely hold on to 80K.

As I said earlier, I think the reasons we have sold off are all actually bullish for ZEC, but when you have these initial moves lower, they often happen in a parallel fashion ie everything goes down. Once the dust settles, the market figures out what it actually wants to own, and the past week of ZEC/BTC going 13% higher shows its decision - I think we see this outperformance continue, and also think if BTC does manage to bounce it's going to be quite interesting for ZEC which should retest its recent highs.

Good luck today.

LLMs have exploded because a simple pre-training task (next token prediction) allows for flexible downstream applications. 

Bio foundation models produce rich representations, but we do not have yet a unified prompting interface to answer biological questions across modalities. What if we could use LLMs as an interface ?

We see AI for biology replaying the vision-language playbook, we are currently at the LLaVA stage.

The recipe is familiar: an LLM on top of a frozen encoder model and an adapter. The encoder learns DNA, proteins or cells instead of images. BioReason plugs Evo2 into Qwen3. CellWhisperer is literally LLaVA on single-cell data. CellScribe borrows AdaLN from diffusion transformers to condition Qwen2.5 on cell embeddings.

The upside is the same as in vision. The foundation model sees structure that may not be known from literature, LLM brings the prior knowledge. RL post-training then applies on top: rbio1 from CZI even uses virtual cell models as soft verifiers.

The failure modes transfer too, in a recent paper @AdaFang_, @marinkazitnik et al. find that when the prompt text already contains hints to the answer, the LLM ignores the embedding. BioReason follows the text over its DNA input in 97.9% of conflicts, and its reasoning traces describe a sequence it did not read. 

Imo the hardest part will be evals (as often in comp bio): prospective evals are hard to build, but evaluating LLMs on retrospective data likely introduce data leakage.

Didn’t expect our omni-LLM research release to coincide with Genie 4, but what better time to share Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-Uni! 

Long name, I know— just call it NLD-Uni.

Our goal: bring multimodal understanding and generation into a unified discrete diffusion language model. Two key ideas make this work:

🧑‍🏫 Cross-paradigm on-policy distillation: learning from autoregressive VLMs for understanding and continuous flow models for visual generation, bridging fundamentally different generation paradigms.

✨ Progressive self-refinement: giving image tokens intermediate states so the model can refine its predictions over multiple steps, improving visual quality.

The result: state-of-the-art performance among unified diffusion LLMs across visual understanding, reasoning, grounding, text-to-image generation, and image editing—with parallel decoding for both image and text tokens.

Our takeaway: discrete tokens offer a promising foundation for bringing strong visual understanding and generation together with efficient diffusion decoding.
